our_perspective: At My Villa, we read a house like La Rêve the way we read any serious work of design: from the material up. Antiques and boiserie give a room its voice, but the structure sets its lifespan. We build in reinforced concrete — the same architectural concrete DGU shaped for Palazzo Grassi and Renzo Piano's Kimbell Art Museum — because the most consequential design decision a client makes is rarely a finish. It is the system beneath the finish: the thing that lets craft endure across generations rather than a single renovation cycle. Permanence is not the enemy of beauty. It is what gives beauty time.
body_html:
A $24 million estate in Beverly Hills is testing a quieter proposition than the glass-and-view spec houses that dominate the hills: that European craft, not raw square footage, is the real luxury. Robb Report reports that La Rêve, designed by Jae Omar, pairs a main residence with a pool house, both layered in antiques and custom detailing drawn from the designer's time living in Paris.

What distinguishes the house, in the reporting, is not a headline amenity but a sensibility: an array of collected antiques and bespoke elements assembled into rooms that read as composed rather than merely outfitted. In a market that often equates value with newness, that is a deliberate counter-move.

What makes La Rêve's design distinct?

In short: it treats the interior as a continuous composition of material and proportion, not a backdrop for views. According to Robb Report, the main residence and pool house are furnished with antiques and custom detailing — the vocabulary of a Parisian apartment translated to a Southern California estate.

The Parisian reference is instructive. The classic Haussmannian interior is organized by things a camera rarely flatters but the body always reads: ceiling height, the rhythm of panelled boiserie, herringbone parquet, stone mantels, enfilade sightlines that pull you from room to room. These are decisions of proportion and craft, and they age into patina rather than out of fashion.

How does Paris shape a Beverly Hills estate?

By importing a logic of layering rather than a style. A Parisian interior is built up over time and reads as collected; the challenge Jae Omar sets himself, per Robb Report, is to achieve that depth at the scale and light of a California estate.

It is a difficult translation. Beverly Hills light is harder and brighter than Paris's grey north exposure; antiques and warm plaster can either anchor a room or feel transplanted. The custom detailing is what bridges the gap — bespoke joinery and surfaces calibrated so the collected pieces sit as if they had always been there.

Done well, this is the opposite of the developer palette of book-matched slabs and identical fixtures. It rewards the kind of attention that does not photograph in a thumbnail but is unmistakable in person.

What does this signal for the LA luxury market?

That the top of the Westside is maturing past spectacle. At $24 million, La Rêve competes with larger, view-forward trophies — and makes the case that a coherent design intelligence is itself the differentiator. Buyers at this tier increasingly want a point of view, not just a square-foot count.

It also rewards designers who can source and compose rather than simply specify. Antiques, custom millwork, and genuine material depth are slower and harder to assemble than a catalogue scheme, and the market is beginning to price that labor as the luxury it is. For architects and agents, the lesson is consistent: proportion, light, and craft remain the durable currency of the Beverly Hills estate, while trend-driven finishes depreciate on contact.
